q.intro.text: A puzzle game moves the tile A B C to A prime B prime C prime, in one single move. Which kind of move was it? Pick an answer, and say how sure you are.

e.intro.text: Let's work it out in four steps. Press each one. The picture moves first, then the board writes it down.

e.step0.text: Every point has a partner. A goes to A prime, B to B prime, C to C prime. Match by the letters, never by where things sit on the page.

e.step1.text: Go round A, B, C: counterclockwise. Go round A prime, B prime, C prime: counterclockwise too. The order is kept, so it's a slide or a turn. A flip would reverse it.

e.step2.text: The three dashed segments meet at the origin, O, and each one is cut exactly in half. Every point stays as far from O as before. That's a half turn: one hundred eighty degrees about O.

e.step3.text: A, at one, one, lands on A prime, at negative one, negative one. Every point does the same: both coordinates change sign. The rule is: x, y goes to negative x, negative y.

e.why.text: Quick check. Why is this a turn, and not a flip?

e.why.ok.text: Yes. A flip reverses the order of the corners. Here the order is kept, and every point turned one hundred eighty degrees about O.

e.why.flip.text: Upside down isn't the test. A half turn looks upside down too. Check the order of the corners: it's kept.

e.why.slide.text: Every motion moves points. In a slide, they all move the same way. Here, A, B and C move in different directions.

t.intro.text: A new tile, and a new move. I'll do the first two steps. Then it's your turn.

t.given.text: Matched: A to A prime, B to B prime, C to C prime. The order A, B, C is counterclockwise in both, so it's kept. It's a slide or a turn.

t.turn.text: Find what stays fixed. Which single motion maps A B C onto A prime B prime C prime?

t.turn.ok.text: Right. A quarter turn: ninety degrees counterclockwise about O. O to A, and O to A prime, make a right angle.

t.turn.reverse.text: Follow A to A prime around O. It goes the other way: counterclockwise.

t.turn.flip.text: A flip would reverse the order of the corners, and here it's kept. It's a turn.

t.rule.text: Write the rule. A, at two, one, went to A prime, at negative one, two. And B, at five, one, went to negative one, five. Which rule does every point follow?

t.rule.ok.text: Right. x, y goes to negative y, x. The coordinates swap, and the new first one changes sign.

t.rule.swap.text: A plain swap would put A prime at one, two. The real A prime is at negative one, two. The new x also changes sign.

t.rule.reverse.text: That rule turns clockwise. Test it on A: it gives one, negative two. But A prime is at negative one, two.

t.apply.text: Use the rule on a new point. Where does D, at four, negative three, land?

t.apply.ok.text: Right. D prime is at three, four. Watch D turn the same quarter turn.

t.apply.swap.text: That only swaps the coordinates. The rule is negative y, x. The first coordinate is minus y.

t.apply.reverse.text: That turns D clockwise. The rule, negative y, x, turns counterclockwise.

t.apply.flip.text: That reflects D across the y-axis. Use the rule: negative y, x.

t.apply.miss.text: Put the numbers in the rule. x is four, y is negative three. So what is negative y, x?

t.len.text: Last check. A B is three units long. How long is A prime B prime?

t.len.ok.text: Right. A turn keeps every length, so A prime B prime is three units, with no measuring.

t.len.remeasure.text: No need to measure. A rigid motion keeps every length, so A prime B prime equals A B: three.

t.len.moved.text: How far the tile travels doesn't matter. The sides keep their lengths. A prime B prime is three.

t.done.text: Back to the puzzle game. The order of the corners was kept, and every point turned about O. So the move was a turn: a one hundred eighty degree rotation.

p.intro.text: Maya uses the rule: x, y goes to two x, negative y. She says: it flips the triangle over the x-axis, so it's a rigid motion. Look, the right angle at A is still a right angle. Is Maya right?

p.build.no.text: Now prove it. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true.

p.build.yes.text: Let's test it. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true, and see where it leads.

p.c1.text: B, at three, one, goes to B prime, at six, negative one. The rule doubles x, and flips the sign of y.

p.c2.text: A B is two squares long, but A prime B prime is four squares long. The side doubled.

p.c3.text: A rigid motion keeps every length. One changed length is enough. Maya's rule is not a rigid motion.

p.done.text: That's a proof. Three claims, each with its reason, and the picture backs every one. One kept angle is not enough.

p.chip.angle.text: That's exactly Maya's mistake. One kept angle doesn't mean every length is kept.

p.chip.size.text: A rigid motion keeps the size too. A wider copy is not a rigid image.

p.chip.slide.text: The points don't all move the same way. B moves three to the right, A only one. It's not a slide.

p.chip.other.text: True, but it's the reason for a different line. Which one makes this line true?
